chapter: The 1920s road: dance style and management
title: Tape 4: recapping Boston, Gibson, Newark and the William Morris deal
summary: He repeats the Boston walkout and the injunctions, dating them to 1923-24, and how William Morris took them for $350.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: You wanted to clear up a few points.

I'd love to clear up a few points, especially where we walked out of the theater in Boston, Massachusetts, which was in the year of '23 or '24 and we went on to other engagements that we set up and we got the appointment for the Standard Theater in Philadelphia with John T. Gibson. For the first time we worked by ourselves as a team of Buck and Bubbles and we left John T. Gibson's and booked in Newark, this is in 1923-24, and we booked in Newark. He filed an injunction against us in Newark.

Nat Nazarro, yeah. And we couldn't go on the stage or work or nothing and we weren't able to draw any money off of the work we already had done and it left us in a bad, precarious position and we had to leave Newark then to further bookings which I
seeked through the William Morris office getting a date in Chicago.
Didn't the William Morris office know that you were being handled by Nazzaro?

Kind of a bargain, I could let them have it for $350 on the assumption that they would book us to Chicago. So they did. To get an act that was worth $1000 for $350 was a good bargain. They weren't going to let that go under no circumstances. I didn't think they would. So we went on to Chicago and we opened up there. And while we were there he extended the injunction against us at one of the theaters there. I think it was at the Grenada Theater on the Balaban & Katz.
